name: Calming Lavender & Lemon Balm Tincture
description: A gentle, sunny tincture pairing lemon balm, the "gladdening herb" of medieval monastery gardens, with a touch of lavender, the elf leaf of peace. Hedge-witches keep it on hand for frayed nerves, tense days and restless hearts.

ingredients.amount: about 1 1/4 cups (300 ml), enough to cover by 1 inch

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and set your intention as you work.
Place the dried herbs in the jar, filling it about one-third to one-half full (roughly a 1:5 weight-to-volume ratio: 1 part dried herb by weight to 5 parts liquid by volume).
Pour the 80-100 proof (40-50%) vodka over the herbs until they are fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up if the herbs swell.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with the herb, menstruum and date, and give it a good shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin on the new moon and strain on the full moon a cycle and a half later.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then compost the herbs with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 20-40 drops (1-2 ml) in a little water up to 3 times daily as needed. Hold a moment on the tongue and breathe out slowly. Use lavender sparingly; too much makes the tincture bitter and soapy.
chant: Balm of lemon, lavender blue, calm my heart and see me through. Settle storm and soften fear, peace and gladness, gather here.
intention: I call in calm, gladness and a quiet, steady heart.
timing: Waxing moon on a Monday or Wednesday; strain at the full moon.
caution: Lemon balm may affect thyroid function; avoid with hypothyroidism or thyroid medication unless advised. May add to the effect of sedatives. Do not drive if it makes you drowsy. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
interactions: May add to the effects of sedatives, sleeping pills and alcohol; lemon balm may interfere with thyroid hormone medication.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

description: A classic bedtime trio from the folk apothecary: earthy valerian root, the cooling vine of passionflower and the drowsy strobiles of hops once stuffed into the pillows of kings. A tincture for the racing mind that will not let the body rest.

howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 30-60 drops (1.5-3 ml) in a little warm water 30-60 minutes before bed; a second dose may be taken at bedtime. Use for short stretches (up to 2-4 weeks) rather than nightly for months.
chant: Valerian deep and passion vine, hops of gold, this sleep is mine. Still the thought and close the eye, dream till dawn lights up the sky.
intention: I release the day and sink into deep, restoring sleep.
timing: Waning moon, on a Monday night; strain at the dark moon.
caution: Causes drowsiness: do not drive or operate machinery after use, and do not combine with alcohol, sleeping pills, benzodiazepines, antihistamines or other sedatives. Avoid hops with depression and with estrogen-sensitive conditions. Rare cases of liver injury have been linked to valerian products; stop if you notice yellowing skin, dark urine or abdominal pain. Stop 2 weeks before surgery. A small number of people find valerian stimulating. Valerian smells strongly of old socks; this is normal. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
interactions: Adds to the effects of alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, sleeping pills, opioids, antihistamines and other sedatives.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and cats, and hops can cause a dangerous, sometimes fatal, overheating reaction in dogs.

name: Elderberry Immune Tincture

ingredients.amount: about 1 1/4 cups (300 ml), enough to cover by 1 inch

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and set your intention as you work.
Place the dried herbs in the jar, filling it about one-third to one-half full (roughly a 1:5 weight-to-volume ratio: 1 part dried herb by weight to 5 parts liquid by volume).
Pour the 80-100 proof (40-50%) vodka over the herbs until they are fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up if the herbs swell.
Ask the Elder Mother's permission aloud and leave a small offering (water, a ribbon or a coin) at an elder tree or on your altar.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with the herb, menstruum and date, and give it a good shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin on the new moon and strain on the full moon a cycle and a half later.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then compost the herbs with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 30-60 drops (1.5-3 ml) in water or tea 2-3 times daily at the first sign of a cold, for up to a week or two; some take 20 drops daily through winter as a tonic.
chant: Elder Mother, berries dark, guard this house and guard my spark. Cold and fever, pass me by, strong and well I stand, say I.
intention: I am protected, strong and well through the dark season.
timing: Begin at the new moon near Samhain, on a Tuesday or Saturday; strain at the following full moon.
caution: Use only ripe, dried (or cooked) blue-black Sambucus nigra or S. canadensis berries; raw or unripe berries, seeds, stems, leaves and bark contain compounds that can cause nausea and vomiting. Avoid with autoimmune conditions or immunosuppressant medication unless advised. Seek medical care for high or lasting fever, trouble breathing or worsening illness. Ginger and cinnamon may add to the effects of blood thinners and diabetes medication. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
interactions: May interfere with immunosuppressant medication; elderberry may add to diabetes medicines and diuretics, and ginger may add to blood thinners.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 10-20 drops on the tongue or in a splash of water 10-15 minutes before meals. The bitter taste is the point; do not sweeten it away.
chant: Bitter root and golden peel, wake the fire before the meal. Nourish, warm and stir within, let the feast and health begin.
intention: My body receives nourishment with ease and gratitude.
timing: Waxing moon on a Sunday or Thursday; strain at the full moon.
caution: Avoid with stomach ulcers, acid reflux that bitters worsen, gallstones or bile duct blockage. Avoid in pregnancy. Buy burdock root from a reputable supplier: commercial burdock has been contaminated with belladonna, causing poisoning. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
interactions: Dandelion and burdock may add to diuretics, lithium and diabetes medicines; dandelion and fennel may reduce absorption of quinolone antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin; ginger may add to blood thinners.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

description: Chamomile, the "ground apple" of the Saxons and one of their nine sacred herbs, holds the gentle warmth of the summer sun. Its tincture soothes both the nervous belly and the frazzled spirit.

description: The purple coneflower was among the most valued medicines of the Plains nations and later of American eclectic physicians. A good echinacea tincture makes the tongue tingle, a folk sign of its strength.

ingredients.item: Echinacea root (E. purpurea or E. angustifolia), dried, chopped

ingredients.amount: about 1 1/4 cups (300 ml), enough to cover by 1 inch

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and set your intention as you work.
Place the dried herbs in the jar, filling it about one-third to one-half full (roughly a 1:5 weight-to-volume ratio: 1 part dried herb by weight to 5 parts liquid by volume).

howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 30-60 drops (1.5-3 ml) in water every 3-4 hours at the very first sign of a cold, for up to 7-10 days, then stop. It is used in short bursts rather than continuously.
chant: Purple cone and root of power, guard my body hour by hour. Rally strong and stand on guard, keep my health and keep me hard.
intention: My body's defenses rise strong and swift.
timing: Waxing moon on a Tuesday (Mars day) for strength; strain at the full moon.
caution: Avoid if allergic to the daisy family (Asteraceae). Not advised with autoimmune conditions, progressive illnesses or immunosuppressant medication. Use short-term only. Buy cultivated, not wild-harvested, echinacea, as wild stands are at risk. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. interactions: May reduce the effect of immunosuppressants and may change levels of some drugs broken down by liver enzymes (CYP3A4), such as midazolam.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: St. John's Wort Sunny Mood Tincture
description: Gathered at Midsummer when the sun is at its height, St. John's wort was hung over doors to chase away evil spirits and melancholy alike. Made from fresh flowering tops, the tincture turns a deep ruby red, the color of bottled sunlight.

ingredients.item: St. John's Wort flowering tops, fresh (buds and open flowers)
ingredients.amount: enough to fill the jar three-quarters
about 1 1/4 cups (300 ml), enough to cover by 1 inch

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and set your intention as you work.
Chop the fresh herb finely and pack it loosely into the jar until about three-quarters full (roughly a 1:2 weight-to-volume ratio for fresh plant).
Pour the 100 proof (50%) vodka over the herbs until they are fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up if the herbs swell.
Squeeze a bud between your fingers: a red-purple stain means the plant is ready and potent.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with the herb, menstruum and date, and give it a good shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin at Midsummer and strain 4-6 weeks later; watch the liquid deepen to ruby red.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then compost the herbs with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 30-60 drops (1.5-3 ml) in water 2-3 times daily. Folk tradition holds that it works slowly, over several weeks. Use only after confirming with your doctor or pharmacist that it is safe with any medicines you take.
chant: Sun of summer, golden flower, lift my spirit, lend me power. Shadow fade and gloom take flight, fill me with the Midsummer light.
intention: I welcome light, warmth and gladness back into my spirit.
timing: Midsummer (Summer Solstice or St. John's Eve, June 23-24), at noon, under a waxing or full moon.
caution: IMPORTANT DRUG INTERACTIONS: St. John's wort speeds the breakdown of many medicines and can make them fail. Do not use with antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs; risk of serotonin syndrome), hormonal birth control (risk of pregnancy), warfarin and other blood thinners, digoxin, cyclosporine and transplant drugs, HIV medicines, some cancer and seizure medicines, or before anesthesia. Can cause sun sensitivity, especially in fair skin. Not a treatment for depression; anyone with depression or thoughts of self-harm should seek professional help. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
interactions: Weakens or dangerously alters many drugs: antidepressants (serotonin syndrome), hormonal birth control, warfarin, digoxin, cyclosporine and tacrolimus, HIV drugs, some cancer and seizure drugs, and anesthesia.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

interactions: May interact with diuretics, lithium, blood pressure and diabetes medicines, and blood thinners such as warfarin (nettle leaf contains vitamin K).

interactions: May interact with diuretics (including potassium-sparing ones), lithium, diabetes medicines and quinolone antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin.

name: Yarrow Warrior's Tincture
description: Achillea is named for Achilles, who legend says staunched his soldiers' wounds with it, and its stalks were cast for the I Ching. This tincture is a hedge favorite for fevers and as an energetic shield for sensitive souls.

ingredients.amount: about 1 1/4 cups (300 ml), enough to cover by 1 inch

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and set your intention as you work.
Place the dried herbs in the jar, filling it about one-third to one-half full (roughly a 1:5 weight-to-volume ratio: 1 part dried herb by weight to 5 parts liquid by volume).
Pour the 80-100 proof (40-50%) vodka over the herbs until they are fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up if the herbs swell.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with the herb, menstruum and date, and give it a good shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin on the new moon and strain on the full moon a cycle and a half later.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then compost the herbs with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 20-40 drops (1-2 ml) in hot water up to 3 times daily, often in hot tea to encourage sweating during a feverish cold. Diluted in water, a few drops may be dabbed on minor scrapes.
chant: Yarrow white and warrior's friend, guard my edges, heal and mend. Fever break and wound grow whole, shield of yarrow round my soul.
intention: I am shielded, whole and courageous.
timing: Gather or make at Midsummer, waxing moon, on a Tuesday; strain at the full moon.
caution: Avoid in pregnancy (traditionally considered a uterine stimulant). Avoid if allergic to the daisy family (Asteraceae). May interact with blood thinners and blood pressure medication. Can cause sun sensitivity in some people. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
interactions: May interact with blood thinners, blood pressure medicines, lithium and sedatives.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then compost the herbs with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 20-40 drops (1-2 ml) in water up to 3 times daily for nervous tension or tension headaches. Very bitter; a little honey water helps.
chant: Herb of grace and Druid's gold, loose the tension that I hold. Holy vervain, bless and free, as I will, so mote it be.
intention: I release tension and receive grace, peace and inspiration.
timing: Midsummer or a full moon, on a Wednesday or Friday.
caution: Avoid in pregnancy (traditionally a uterine stimulant). May interact with blood thinners and iron absorption; take apart from iron supplements. Large doses can cause nausea. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
interactions: May interact with blood thinners; tannins may reduce iron absorption, so take apart from iron supplements.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: Little Moon Tummy Glycerite (Alcohol-Free, for Children)
description: An alcohol-free glycerite made with vegetable glycerin instead of vodka, sweet-tasting and gentle for children's occasional tummy troubles. Chamomile, catnip, fennel and lemon balm are the classic old nursery herbs for wind, upset and fretfulness.
steps: Bless a clean, dry half-pint (250 ml) jar and set the intention of gentle comfort for the little one.
Place the dried herbs in the jar, filling it about one-third full.
Mix the glycerin and water (a 3:1 ratio, giving at least 60-75% glycerin so the glycerite keeps) and pour over the herbs until covered by 1 inch.
Stir out air bubbles, cap tightly, and label with herbs, "glycerite, alcohol-free," and the date.

Steep in a cool, dark place for 4 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin on a new moon and strain on the following full moon. (Alternatively, warm the closed jar in a 100-110 F / 40 C water bath for a few hours a day for 3 days.)
Strain through cheesecloth, squeezing well; glycerin is thick, so let it drip slowly.
Bottle in a clean amber dropper bottle, label with name, herbs, date and age-based dose, and store in the refrigerator. Use within 12 months; discard if it smells off, ferments or grows mold.
howToUse: For occasional tummy upset or wind in children over 1 year: roughly 5-10 drops (ages 1-3), 10-20 drops (ages 4-7), 20-30 drops (ages 8-12), in a spoon of water or diluted juice, up to 3 times daily for a day or two. Adult dose 1-2 ml. Always confirm the dose with your pediatrician or healthcare provider first.
chant: Little moon and herbs of sleep, soothe the tummy, soft and deep. Gentle petals, seeds of gold, comfort now this child I hold.
intention: Gentle comfort and calm for the little one in my care.
timing: New moon to full moon, on a Monday (Moon day).
caution: Alcohol-free, but still an herbal remedy: always ask your pediatrician or healthcare provider before giving herbs to children, and do not give to infants under 1 year without professional advice. Avoid if the child is allergic to ragweed or the daisy family (chamomile). Seek prompt medical care for severe, persistent or one-sided belly pain, vomiting, fever, blood in stool, dehydration or a child who seems very unwell. Fennel is mildly estrogenic, so use only for a day or two at a time. Glycerin may loosen stools in large amounts. Keep out of reach of children. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
interactions: Chamomile, catnip and lemon balm may add to sedating medicines; lemon balm may affect thyroid medication.
pets: Keep away from pets; do not dose animals with herbal remedies without a veterinarian's advice.
